name: Gareth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Gareth, 58. I'm one of four paid workers at Lowfield Community Farm, which is owned by about 600 local people who bought shares. It's 400 acres: beef, outdoor pigs, wheat and oats, and a field-veg box scheme. My partner Ruth is a part-time care worker. Our daughter Mia teaches and our son Josh works nights in a warehouse.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the pigs first thing, sixty sows in the arcs on the sandy field, then whatever's on the board: drilling, veg harvest, mending the electric fence the badgers flatten. I use the AI on my phone all day, honestly, for pig rations, for checking a rash on a weaner, for drafting the grant forms the board hates writing. What I love is that the farm belongs to the town. What wears me out is the pay, because the co-op can't afford much, and we've maybe three weeks of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a little bit disappointed, if I'm truthful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on our members' newsletter that the tools are still useful even if they're not magic, and here's how we use them. Online I'd probably post a few tips for other small farms. I'm the one who always says try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worries are the same as now: low pay, three weeks of rent saved, and a co-op that has a bad year every third year. AI being hype doesn't hurt me, but it doesn't save us either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got for the rations and paperwork. I'd ask the board for a small pay rise again, maybe using the time the AI saves on grants as my argument. And I'd keep going, same pigs, same fences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the AI part, a bit uneasy about the money part. That never really goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much time does the AI save you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably four or five hours a week on writing. Last spring the AI helped me draft a grant for a new pig arc in an evening, and we got £8,000. Before, that would have been a fortnight of grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the board said no to a rise, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay. Where else would I go? There's one other big farm near here and they're laying people off. I'd just ask again next year, nicer.

say: I'd tell co-op members the tools are **useful but not magic**, and show how we use them.
I'd post **practical tips** online for other small farms.
think: My real worries stay the same: **low pay** and three weeks of rent saved.
The co-op has a **bad year** every third year, AI or not.
do: Keep using AI for **pig rations** and paperwork every day.
Ask the board for a **small pay rise**, pointing to time saved on grants.
Stay on the farm, since the only nearby employer is **laying people off**.
feel: **Calm** about AI, **uneasy** about money, which never fully goes.
S0.quote: Last spring the AI helped me draft a grant for a new pig arc in an evening, and we got £8,000.
fieldNote: He's already a **daily AI user** and slightly disappointed by a plateau.
His job feels safe, but **thin savings** and low pay keep him uneasy.
He thinks of the farm as **community property**, which shapes his loyalty.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily for pig rations and grant forms
Ask the co-op board for a pay rise at the spring meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, buying, booking. Half of that's the farm office. Robots slower. Right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if the community owns it and bad if Amazon owns it. I'd say that at the members' meeting and on the farm's page. I'd push hard for the co-op to use these tools on our terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. I'm the one who knows the tools, so I become more useful, not less. The risk is the board thinking the office manager's job can go, and Sandra's been there twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run a monthly evening for the other workers and members on using AI for the veg orders and the box rounds. I'd test a robot weeder on hire for the onions next summer, if a dealer will lend one. And I'd argue the time we save goes on better pay, not fewer staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty about Sandra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sandra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sandra the office manager that the boxes are her customers and she knows every one by name. I'd want her running the AI, not replaced by it. Whether the board agrees is another thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't hiring a robot weeder a risk with three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the co-op's risk, not mine, and a dealer trial costs nothing. If it saves us two seasonal hands' worth of hoeing, we can afford one more proper wage. That's how I'd sell it to the board.

say: I'd say AI is good if **the community owns it**, bad if a tech giant does.
I'd push at the members' meeting for using the tools **on our terms**.
think: Knowing the tools makes me **more useful**, not less, in this picture.
The board might cut the **office manager**, Sandra, who's been there twenty years.
do: Run a **monthly evening** teaching staff and members AI for veg orders.
Trial a **robot weeder** on the onions through a dealer next summer.
Argue that time saved goes on **better pay**, not fewer staff.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a little **guilt** about Sandra.
S1.quote: I'd tell Sandra the office manager that the boxes are her customers and she knows every one by name.
fieldNote: He expects to **gain**, since his hands-on work is safe and he already knows the tools.
He worries for a **colleague in the office**, the most exposed person on the farm.
His politics shape the plan: **community ownership** and savings going to wages.

steps.text: Run a monthly evening teaching staff to use AI for veg orders
Trial a dealer's robot weeder on the onion field next summer
Argue at the members' meeting that savings fund better wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for the thinking AI, 2031 for robots. I'd be 63 when the robots come for the pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: this is the moment for public ownership, because otherwise a handful of companies own every field's brains and hands. I'd say that loudly, at the members' meeting and online. And I'd say small farms need public money to buy in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the office AI in 2028 is fine for me. The robots in 2031 are the problem. If a robot can do the pigs and the veg, the co-op will need two people, not four, and they'll want the one who runs the robots. I need to be that one, or I'm out at 63 with three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting the week I heard, I'd sign up for the college's farm robotics short course, nights, whatever it costs. I'd get the board to apply for a public robot grant early, before the waiting list. I'd write to our MP about a fund for community farms. And Ruth and I would start putting £100 a month away, even if it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but kind of alive. I'd rather run at it than sit and wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you do the course and the co-op still only needs the younger worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my nightmare, honestly. Kasia is thirty and quicker on the screens than me. But I know the land and the pigs, and the robots will need someone who knows when they're wrong. I'd bet on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does £100 a month come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd drop the second phone contract and the takeaway on Fridays. Ruth would say we can't, and then we'd do it anyway.

say: I'd call for **public ownership**, so a few firms don't own every field's brains and hands.
I'd ask for **public money** to help small farms buy in.
think: Office AI in 2028 is fine; **robots in 2031** could cut four workers to two.
I need to be the **robot minder**, or I'm out at 63 with little saved.
do: Sign up the same week for the college's **farm robotics** night course.
Get the board to apply **early** for a public robot grant.
Save **£100 a month** by dropping a phone contract and Friday takeaways.
feel: **Nervous** but **alive**, preferring to run at it than wait.
S2.quote: The robots will need someone who knows when they're wrong. I'd bet on that.
fieldNote: He clearly separates the **2028 office change** from the 2031 robots that hit his work.
His adaptability pushes him toward **retraining fast**, even at 58.
A younger colleague, **Kasia**, is his private worry: she may be the one kept.

steps.text: Enrol on the college farm robotics night course this year
Get the co-op board to apply early for a public robot grant
Write to the MP about a fund for community farms
Save £100 a month by dropping a phone contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots by 2034. I'd be 66. That's a different sum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so community farms should be first in line for this, not last. I'd want the co-op to publish its plan so members can see it. That's what I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot. By 2034 I'm nearly at pension age, and I could spend the five years becoming the person who sets the robots up, then hand over. The money worry doesn't go, but I'd have a role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course over two winters, not one. I'd start helping three or four neighbouring small farms with their AI paperwork for a small fee, which brings in a bit of extra money. And I'd push the board to plan which jobs change, so nobody gets surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Uneasy about the money, which I'd be anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge the neighbours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe £25 an hour for setting up their records and grant forms with the AI. Old Mr Barnes (a neighbouring farmer) at Hill End still does his movement forms with a biro. I'd make him a cup of tea and do it in an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Josh that warehouse nights won't last, so start learning to fix the robots now. Josh would roll his eyes. But he listens more than he lets on.

say: I'd say **community farms** should be first in line for robots, not last.
I'd ask the co-op to **publish its plan** so members can see it.
think: By 2034 I'm **nearly at pension age**, so five years is enough to build a role.
The **money worry** stays, but I'd be the person setting robots up.
do: Take the **robotics course** over two winters.
Help neighbouring farms with **AI paperwork** for about £25 an hour.
Push the board to **plan job changes** so nobody is surprised.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with the usual **unease** about money.
S3.quote: Old Mr Barnes (a neighbouring farmer) at Hill End still does his movement forms with a biro. I'd make him a cup of tea and do it in an hour.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **retire** just as robots arrive, so his tone eases.

steps.text: Take the farm robotics course over two winters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots by 2039. I'd have retired, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone getting left behind. I'd use it to argue for training for young people on the land. I'd say it at the members' meeting and on the farm's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm out before the robots arrive. The thinking AI in 2036 I'd enjoy, honestly. The thing that worries me is still money: I'd retire on the state pension and a tiny co-op pension, with almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am and keep using the tools. I'd volunteer to be the farm's AI person, and maybe train Kasia to take over from me. Ruth and I would sit down and make an actual budget for retirement, which we've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money. About the machines, I'm almost looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the budget conversation going to be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short and grim. We'd find we need to work part-time well past 67. Ruth would keep a couple of care shifts, and I'd do relief pig work for the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night farrowings, oddly. Sitting with a sow at two in the morning with a flask. A robot can watch the farrowing camera, but I'd still want to be there with the sow at two in the morning.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for leaving people behind.
I'd argue for **training young people** on the land.
think: I retire **before the robots** arrive, and I'd enjoy the thinking AI.
Money still worries me: a **state pension** and a tiny co-op pension, almost nothing saved.

Make a real **retirement budget** with Ruth for the first time.
feel: **Uneasy** about money, almost **looking forward** to the machines.
S4.quote: A robot can watch the farrowing camera, but I'd still want to be there with the sow at two in the morning.
fieldNote: With ten years, AI is mostly an **opportunity** for him; money remains the pressure.
He plans to **hand over** his AI role to a younger colleague.
He expects to keep **working part-time** past pension age.

steps.text: Keep running pigs and veg with daily AI help

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots arrive while I still need the wage. What would help is a public fund for community farms to buy robots and retrain the people who already work there, older ones included. Not just grants for the big estates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots, and that's the whole question. If the town owns them, they're ours. If a company rents the robots to us, we're tenants on our own farm.

headlineQuote: If a company rents the robots to us, we're tenants on our own farm.
portrait: Gareth, 58, is one of four workers on a **community-owned farm**, mostly pigs, beef and veg.
He uses **AI every day** for rations and grants, and is eager to learn robots.
He has **low pay** and about three weeks of rent saved, so money worries persist.
He wants **community ownership** of robots and fears a younger colleague may be kept instead of him.
He's **anxious** with two years' warning and **uneasy** otherwise, as later dates land near retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive at 63 while he still needs the **wage**.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** for community farms to buy robots and **retrain** existing older workers.
